approaches.name: Ilioinguinal approach to the acetabulum
approaches.corridor: Three-window extraperitoneal exposure around the iliopsoas, femoral neurovascular bundle, and spermatic cord or round ligament

procedure_applications.condition: Anterior wall, anterior column, both-column, or selected transverse exposure is required

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the injured limb included in the field so hip flexion can relax the iliopsoas and femoral neurovascular structures.

setup.text: Prepare the lower abdomen, hemipelvis, and operative leg; place and confirm a urinary catheter so the bladder can be identified and protected during medial-window development.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the iliac crest, anterior superior iliac spine, inguinal ligament, pubic tubercle, and pubic symphysis.

incision.text: Use a curved incision along the iliac crest and inguinal region that can extend medially just proximal to the pubic symphysis according to the windows required.

superficial_interval.text: Elevate the abdominal wall from the iliac crest, open the external-oblique aponeurosis above the inguinal canal, and mobilize the spermatic cord or round ligament medially.

deep_interval.text: Develop three windows: internal iliac fossa lateral to iliopsoas, pelvic brim between iliopsoas/femoral nerve and femoral vessels, and the medial retropubic window beside rectus and the cord or round ligament.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue, external-oblique aponeurosis and inguinal structures, iliacus and iliopsoas mobilization, iliopectineal fascia, then subperiosteal anterior pelvic and acetabular exposure.

structures_encountered.text: The exposure encounters the lateral femoral cutaneous and ilioinguinal nerves, iliopsoas and femoral nerve, external iliac/femoral vessels, spermatic cord or round ligament, and iliopectineal fascia.

structures_at_risk.text: Femoral and external iliac vessels, femoral nerve, lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, ilioinguinal nerve, bladder, spermatic cord or round ligament, and corona-mortis anastomoses require direct identification and protection.

danger_zones.text: Divide the iliopectineal fascia only under direct vision between gently mobilized vessels medially and iliopsoas/femoral nerve laterally; minimize circumferential vascular dissection.

retraction_hazards.text: Continuously monitor medial vessel retraction and avoid prolonged compression of the femoral neurovascular bundle; protect the bladder with controlled packing in the space of Retzius.

exposure.text: Exposes the internal iliac fossa from the sacroiliac joint to the iliopectineal eminence, pelvic brim and quadrilateral surface, and superior pubic ramus to the symphysis through three windows.

limitations.text: Reduction is primarily indirect because the articular surface is not directly visualized; complex intrapelvic work may be better addressed through an anterior intrapelvic modification.

extensions.text: The third window can be expanded across the midline into an anterior intrapelvic exposure of the quadrilateral surface and posterior column.

indications.text: Used for anterior-wall and anterior-column fractures, many both-column patterns, and selected transverse or associated acetabular fractures requiring broad anterior access.

relative_contraindications.text: Prior inguinal or femoral hernia surgery and active hernia can complicate the second window; consider limiting that window or selecting an alternative exposure.

implant_implications.text: Implant placement is performed through separate windows around the neurovascular bundle; plate contour and screw trajectories must be planned without directly seeing the articular reduction.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Maintain access for AP, obturator-oblique, and iliac-oblique imaging because reduction is indirect and intra-articular penetration must be excluded.

closure.text: Reconstruct the conjoint tendon and inguinal floor without trapping cord structures, repair external-oblique and rectus fascia, and securely reattach the abdominal wall to the iliac crest.

complications.text: Complications include major vascular or femoral-nerve injury, lateral femoral cutaneous neuropathy, lymphatic injury, bladder or cord injury, inguinal hernia, infection, and wound morbidity.

bailouts.text: If safe vessel mobilization or a required window cannot be achieved, stop blind retraction and convert to the planned intrapelvic or alternative exposure rather than forcing access.

Why is acetabular reduction indirect through the classic ilioinguinal approach?
questions.answer: The articular surface is not directly visualized; reduction relies on restoration of extra-articular anatomy and imaging.

approaches.name: Anterior intrapelvic approach (modified Stoppa)
approaches.corridor: Extraperitoneal retropubic corridor deep to rectus abdominis along the inner pelvis and quadrilateral surface

procedure_applications.condition: Direct intrapelvic access to the quadrilateral surface, anterior column, or medial posterior column is required

positioning.text: Position supine on a radiolucent table with the injured leg in the field and the hip and knee flexed enough to relax iliopsoas and external iliac vessels.

setup.text: Place a urinary catheter, prepare the lower abdomen and hemipelvis, and arrange fluoroscopy for AP and Judet views before incision.

surface_landmarks.text: Identify the pubic symphysis, linea alba, rectus borders, inguinal ligament, and iliac crest if a lateral window may be added.

incision.text: Use a transverse Pfannenstiel incision just proximal to the pubic symphysis, with a separate lateral-window extension when upper anterior-column exposure is needed.

superficial_interval.text: Open the rectus fascia at the linea alba, separate the rectus bellies, and remain strictly in the preperitoneal space.

deep_interval.text: Develop the inner surface of the superior pubic ramus and pelvic brim subperiosteally, mobilizing obturator structures and elevating obturator internus to expose the quadrilateral surface.

layers.text: Skin and subcutaneous tissue, anterior rectus sheath and linea alba, rectus separation, preperitoneal retropubic space, periosteum and obturator internus, then quadrilateral surface and pelvic brim.

structures_encountered.text: Corona-mortis vessels, external iliac vessels and iliopsoas laterally, obturator neurovascular bundle, bladder, peritoneum, pelvic floor, and lumbosacral trunk define the exposure.

structures_at_risk.text: The obturator neurovascular bundle, corona mortis, external iliac vein, bladder, peritoneum, pelvic floor, and lumbosacral trunk are at risk during intrapelvic dissection and retraction.

danger_zones.text: Identify and control corona-mortis vessels before deeper lateral mobilization, and protect the obturator bundle with a malleable retractor while elevating obturator internus.

retraction_hazards.text: Prevent retractor slippage into the pelvis; avoid avulsion of variably tethered obturator vessels and direct pressure on external iliac vein, bladder, or lumbosacral trunk.

exposure.text: Directly exposes the pubic symphysis, superior pubic ramus, quadrilateral surface, pelvic brim, and medial posterior column; a lateral window completes upper anterior-column exposure.

limitations.text: The upper iliac wing and sacroiliac region require a lateral window, and distal internal-iliac branching can restrict safe posterior quadrilateral-surface dissection.

extensions.text: Add an iliac-crest lateral window to expose the internal iliac fossa, sacral ala, anterior sacroiliac joint, and upper anterior column.

indications.text: Useful for anterior-column, both-column, quadrilateral-surface, and selected transverse acetabular patterns requiring direct medial buttress access.

relative_contraindications.text: Use caution after extensive lower-abdominal surgery or when vascular anatomy, intrapelvic scarring, or the fracture target prevents safe extraperitoneal access.

implant_implications.text: The approach permits direct infrapectineal buttress plating of the quadrilateral surface while protecting obturator and external iliac structures from clamps, drills, and screws.

fluoroscopy_implications.text: Preserve AP and Judet imaging access to assess column reduction, posterior-column screws, and intra-articular penetration.

closure.text: Close linea alba and rectus fascia while protecting bladder and peritoneum; reconstruct each lateral-window fascial layer when used.

complications.text: Complications include obturator or external-iliac neurovascular injury, major corona-mortis bleeding, bladder or peritoneal injury, hernia, infection, and wound complications.

bailouts.text: If bleeding obscures the field or safe mobilization is impossible, pack and obtain vascular control before proceeding; add the lateral window rather than forcing upper-column access intrapelvically.
